[1. arXiv:2610.00820v1]
On-the-fly Weight Generation: A Hypernetwork Proof of Concept on ARC-1D

Abstract: General-purpose models can adapt to many tasks from context, while specialised models can execute individual functions with less capacity. Yet obtaining such specialists requires task-specific training or adaptation. We ask whether they can instead be generated directly from a few demonstrations. Using ARC-1D as a controlled testbed, we show that individual transformations can be represented by tiny specialist models, and that a hypernetwork can generate their parameters from context. The generated parameters form a structured weight space, while the resulting specialists show partial compositional generalisation and generalisation to transformations not seen during training. In both settings, removing explicit task identifiers improves generalisation beyond the training transformations. Together, these results provide a proof of concept that few-shot task context can be compiled on-the-fly into compact executable model parameters, and that the resulting weight space can support reuse and generalisation beyond known functions.

Section: 4.2 SpecialisedModels Require Less Capacity

We first ask how much capacity is required to represent an individual ARC-1D transformation. Recent results show that small recurrent models can solve complex ARC tasks [Wang et al., 2025a, Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025, Gao et al., 2025], motivating us to use a deliberately small target architecture. We progressively simplify a Transformer with RoPE [Su et al., 2024] to the three-layer Canon Transformer [Allen-Zhu, 2025] used throughout our subsequent experiments. Our aim is not to identify an optimal architecture, but to obtain a simple target model whose capacity can be varied directly. Full architecture configurations are provided in Appendix Table 3.
Figure 3 reveals a clear cost to sharing parameters. Individual models saturate at 98.9% accuracy with only 2.4K parameters, while the same sized architecture reaches 74.0% when trained jointly, even when given the transformation identity. Increasing capacity closes this gap, suggesting that individual transformations are cheap to represent but require additional capacity when stored in shared parameters. This penalty is concentrated in a few transformations (Figure 4); most remain near their individual ceiling, while Flip, Mirror and Moves 1, 3 fall from 100%. We provide figures of the alternative model sizes in Appendix C.

These results separate the capacity required to represent multiple functions in shared parameters from that required to execute an individual function. This motivates separating task inference from execution: rather than storing all transformations in shared target-model parameters, a hypernetwork can infer the transformation from the support set and instantiate a small standalone predictor to execute it. This leads to our central question: given that a tiny network can represent each solution, can a hypernetwork learn to generate those networks from examples?

[2. arXiv:2610.00791v1]
Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS): Reducing Representational Complexity for Enterprise AI

Abstract: Enterprise information is represented through artifacts shaped by applications, projects, technologies, organizational boundaries, and local requirements. These structures accumulate over time, creating representational complexity that must be maintained by the enterprise and interpreted by information consumers and AI systems. This paper introduces Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS) as reducing unnecessary representational complexity while preserving required information within a defined scope, and Enterprise Representation Complexity (ERC), a representation-neutral model for comparing complexity across representation states.   ERC characterizes representational extent through four dimensions: Representation Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, and Supporting Sources. Objects, Interactions, and Behaviors form dependent categories, while Supporting Sources characterize representation exposure. ERC is defined at representation and task levels, enabling comparison and distinguishing architectural simplification from retrieval optimization.   The paper develops two consequences of ERS. First, representational structures create lifecycle obligations for maintenance, governance, dependencies, change, enhancement, and operation. An economic model distinguishes recurring global representation cost, recurring task-level cost, and one-time transformation cost, enabling evaluation over a defined time horizon. Second, reductions in task-level ERC reduce the representational extent an AI system must identify, relate, and interpret. Text-to-SQL research provides evidence that reduced schema and reasoning complexity can improve reasoning accuracy.   ERC is not a universal complexity, performance, or cost metric. It provides measurable architectural variables for comparing representational alternatives, transformation effects, economic outcomes, and AI reasoning performance.

Section: 8.7 What Can Increase Cost

ERS does not imply that every economic component decreases. Cost can increase only where the transformation introduces a genuinely new obligation, shifts an existing obligation into a more costly form, or incurs a one-time transformation expense. Examples include a new abstraction or mediation service that must be operated, processing that is relocated rather than eliminated, or other persistent mechanisms required specifically by R1. These costs are captured in NT rather than inferred merely from the fact that a resulting Object or Behavior is richer than one of its predecessors.
The transformation fromR0 to R1 also incurs a one-time implementation cost. This cost is economically important but should be separated from the recurring cost of the resulting representation because it is not incurred indefinitely.

[3. arXiv:2610.00791v1]
Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS): Reducing Representational Complexity for Enterprise AI

Abstract: Enterprise information is represented through artifacts shaped by applications, projects, technologies, organizational boundaries, and local requirements. These structures accumulate over time, creating representational complexity that must be maintained by the enterprise and interpreted by information consumers and AI systems. This paper introduces Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS) as reducing unnecessary representational complexity while preserving required information within a defined scope, and Enterprise Representation Complexity (ERC), a representation-neutral model for comparing complexity across representation states.   ERC characterizes representational extent through four dimensions: Representation Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, and Supporting Sources. Objects, Interactions, and Behaviors form dependent categories, while Supporting Sources characterize representation exposure. ERC is defined at representation and task levels, enabling comparison and distinguishing architectural simplification from retrieval optimization.   The paper develops two consequences of ERS. First, representational structures create lifecycle obligations for maintenance, governance, dependencies, change, enhancement, and operation. An economic model distinguishes recurring global representation cost, recurring task-level cost, and one-time transformation cost, enabling evaluation over a defined time horizon. Second, reductions in task-level ERC reduce the representational extent an AI system must identify, relate, and interpret. Text-to-SQL research provides evidence that reduced schema and reasoning complexity can improve reasoning accuracy.   ERC is not a universal complexity, performance, or cost metric. It provides measurable architectural variables for comparing representational alternatives, transformation effects, economic outcomes, and AI reasoning performance.

Section: 13 Conclusion

ERS treats representational complexity as an architectural condition that can be deliberately reduced rather than merely navigated. It is defined as an information-preserving transformation that reduces unnecessary representation relative to a defined enterprise information scope. ERC makes representational complexity measurable through separate functions for each dimension:
This paper operationalizes these functions using cardinality, providing a simple, observable, and technology-independent measure of representational size. The multidimensional structure preserves differences among representational categories rather than collapsing them into an unsupported scalar measure. Representation-level ERC characterizes the broader enterprise representation, while task-level ERC characterizes the minimum representation required to satisfy a particular information requirement.
ERS also provides a basis for examining the consequences of representational design. Representation creates recurring obligations associated with maintenance, governance, security, dependency management, change, and operation. At the task level, representation may affect context construction, inference, validation, and remediation. ERC does not assign economic cost, computational/resource burden, or reasoning performance to these conditions; it provides common architectural variables through which their relationships can be observed and compared. Representation Utilization and Representation Change Surface extend this analysis by distinguishing what is actually used and how broadly subsequent change propagates without incorporating those consequences into ERC itself.
For AI, ERS addresses a problem upstream of retrieval. Rather than accepting existing representational complexity and focusing only on selecting relevant context, simplification changes the representation from which context is derived. Reductions in task-level ERC may therefore reduce the representation an AI system must identify, relate, and interpret. Existing Text-to-SQL research supports the broader proposition that representational design can affect reasoning performance, while the specific relationships among ERC dimensions, accuracy, task economics, validation, and remediation remain empirical questions.
26
Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS)
A PREPRINT
ERS therefore establishes an architectural objective, while ERC provides a measurement structure for evaluating progress toward it. ERS does not presume that fewer representational structures necessarily produce lower cost, greater agility, higher utilization, or better AI reasoning. Instead, it enables alternative representations to be measured consistently and their consequences evaluated empirically.
More broadly, repeated ERC measurement can turn individual architectural decisions into cumulative organizational evidence. Observations across representations, tasks, workloads, and transformations can reveal which representational conditions are consistently associated with utilization, reasoning performance, lifecycle obligations, and change effort. Those relationships can subsequently inform transformation priorities, resource allocation, and prospective architectural decisions. In this sense, ERS provides not only an approach to reducing unnecessary representation, but a basis for an enduring process of measurement, learning, and continuous representational improvement.
